Almug
AL-mug
noun
From the Hebrew almuggim, appearing by metathesis as algummim in Chronicles — a costly imported timber, most probably the red sandalwood of the East, close-grained, fragrant, and fit alike for building and for the making of instruments of music.

Biblical Definition

Almug is the finest timber named in Scripture, and it is named only in the building of the house of the LORD. Hiram’s navy fetched it from Ophir with gold and precious stones: “the navy also of Hiram, that brought gold from Ophir, brought in from Ophir great plenty of almug trees, and precious stones” (1Ki 10:11). What Solomon did with it is the point. “And the king made of the almug trees pillars for the house of the LORD, and for the king’s house, harps also and psalteries for singers: there came no such almug trees, nor were seen unto this day” (1Ki 10:12). Note the order: the house of the LORD first, the king’s house second. The best of the best went to the sanctuary before it went to the palace, and what remained went to praise. The Chronicler records the same, calling the timber algum and the work terraces: “and there were none such seen before in the land of Judah” (2Ch 9:11). Here is the wealth of the nations sailing to Zion by the LORD’s ordering, exactly as Isaiah foretold — the glory of Lebanon brought “to beautify the place of my sanctuary” (Isa 60:13). And here is worship built and sung upon rarest wood, that the congregation might have pillars beneath it and harps before it. Yet the temple was a shadow; the substance is Christ, in whom “dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

A rare and costly timber brought from Ophir, used for the pillars of the temple and for harps and psalteries.

ALMUG, a precious wood of the East, brought by Solomon’s navy from Ophir; called algum in Chronicles.

From the Hebrew almuggim / algummim, most probably red sandalwood.

It is close-grained and fragrant, fit for building and for instruments of music.

Solomon made of it pillars for the house of the LORD and for the king’s house (1Ki 10:12).

Of the same wood were made harps and psalteries for the singers.

Key Scripture

1Ki 10:11 — "And the navy also of Hiram, that brought gold from Ophir, brought in from Ophir great plenty of almug trees, and precious stones."

1Ki 10:12 — "And the king made of the almug trees pillars for the house of the LORD, and for the king's house, harps also and psalteries for singers: there came no such almug trees, nor were seen unto this day."

2Ch 9:10 — "And the servants also of Huram, and the servants of Solomon, which brought gold from Ophir, brought algum trees and precious stones."

2Ch 9:11 — "And the king made of the algum trees terraces to the house of the LORD, and to the king's palace, and harps and psalteries for singers: and there were none such seen before in the land of Judah."

Modern Corruption

The rarest timber went to God’s house first — a rebuke both to worship on the cheap and to worship as spectacle.

expand to see more

Two opposite corruptions meet at the almug. The first is worship on the leftovers: the congregation that gives God its scraps of time, its least prepared men, its unconsidered singing, its afterthought offering, while its own houses are panelled. Haggai named that sin plainly — “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4) — and Malachi named it sharper still, when the blind and the lame beast was brought to the altar and the governor would not have accepted it (Mal 1:8). Solomon’s ships fetched the best wood on earth and unloaded it at the temple before the palace. That order is the standing rebuke.

The second corruption runs the other way: worship as spectacle, where the “best” is defined by the eye and the ear of the consumer, and the house of God becomes a stage judged by production. The regulative principle answers both. God Himself appoints what He will have in His worship, and Solomon built by a pattern given, not by taste invented (1Ch 28:11–12, 19). Under the New Testament the appointed elements are plain — the reading and preaching of the Word, prayer, the singing of psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, the two ordinances, and the offering — and the “almug” the Lord now asks is the best of those: careful preaching, hearty congregational singing, reverent administration. The temple’s costly pillars have given place to a costlier building, for believers are now “an holy temple in the Lord” (Eph 2:21), and the finest timber He asks for is a living one.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word names a rare imported timber reserved for the house of the LORD and for praise.

expand to see more

Almug — Hebrew almuggim; algummim in Chronicles.

Most probably the red sandalwood of the East, fragrant and close-grained.

It came from Ophir in Hiram’s navy with gold and precious stones (1Ki 10:11).

Solomon made of it pillars for the house of the LORD before the king’s house.

Of the same wood were made harps and psalteries for the singers (1Ki 10:12).

Usage

"Almug came from Ophir with the gold — and went to the sanctuary before the palace."

"The rarest wood in the world was cut into harps: praise gets the best timber."

"There came no such almug trees again; the temple had the finest of the earth once."
